record.body:
A healthcare access report needs to show the barriers people face when they try to get care.

I built Health-Access-for-PWDs to bring communication support, physical access and affordability into one dashboard. A reader can examine each barrier, compare groups and see how the indicators stand against the targets used in the project.

This is a portfolio demonstration using simulated data. The figures illustrate the analysis; they are not findings from a new survey or estimates for Nigeria.

The dashboard lets you filter by state, disability group and facility level. You can narrow the view to a particular group and check the barriers shown for that selection. The number of records and the average service-quality rating update with it.

For communication support, the indicators cover interpreter availability and accessible information. Physical access includes facilities such as accessible toilets. Financial difficulty appears separately, so cost remains visible alongside the other barriers to care.

I put each headline indicator's current value beside its target. That gives a program manager a clear starting point for a review: the size of the gap, the group being considered and the service issue that needs attention.

I also kept the number of records visible. A percentage can look convincing on its own. Seeing how many people it represents helps a reader judge how much weight to give it and whether more information is needed.

For me, the useful part of this dashboard is being able to move from an overview to a specific issue. A team could use that structure to examine communication support in one group, discuss physical access in another, and explain the evidence behind a proposed priority.

Using real survey data would require checking how responses were collected, who was included and whether the comparisons are fair. The demonstration shows how I would organise the review; it does not establish which communities should receive funding.

Before recommending an action, I would check the underlying responses and discuss the apparent gap with the people affected.
record.topic: Making healthcare access barriers easier to examine
